subject: maths
title: Year 4 Perimeter and Area
seo_title: Year 4 Perimeter and Area Worksheets: Free Maths with Answer Key (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Recognise ways of measuring and approximating the perimeter and area of shapes and enclosed spaces, using appropriate formal and informal units
meta_desc: Free Year 4 perimeter and area worksheets for the Australian Curriculum (AC9M4M02): add the sides of rectangles and rectilinear shapes, find missing sides, count squares and half squares, estimate irregular areas on a grid and choose cm² or m². 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Perimeter is the distance around the edge. Area is the number of squares inside.
key_sub: Add every side to find the perimeter, in cm or m. Count whole and half squares to find the area, in cm² or m². For curved shapes, count squares that are half or more covered.
body_html:
Perimeter and area

Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape. It is a length, so it is in cm or m.

Area is the space inside a shape. In Year 4 we find it by counting squares. If each square is 1 cm² (1 square centimetre), the area is in cm². Big spaces such as a floor are measured in m² (square metres).

Perimeter: add all the sides

Add every side. A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides.

Perimeter on a grid

Count the sides of the squares around the edge, not the squares. A corner square has 2 sides on the edge.

Find a missing side

In a shape with right angles, like an L, the short sides on one side add up to the long side opposite.

Example

A garden bed is 12 m long and 5 m wide. How much edging goes around it?

12 + 5 + 12 + 5 = 34. Or 12 + 5 = 17, then double it: 17 + 17 = 34.

Answer: 34 m

Area: count squares and half squares

Count the squares inside, row by row. Two half squares make one whole square.

Counting in rows is quicker: 3 rows of 5 squares is 3 × 5 = 15 squares.

Estimate the area of a curved shape

Curved shapes do not fit the squares exactly, so we estimate. Count each whole square. Count a square as 1 if half or more is covered. Leave out squares that are less than half covered.

Choose the unit

MeasuringSmall thingsBig things
Perimeter (a length)cm: a photo, a bookm: a garden bed, a court
Area (squares inside)cm²: a stamp, a pagem²: a classroom floor, a backyard

Informal units work too, such as sticky notes or tiles, but everyone must use the same size square.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding only two sides (9 + 4 = 13 cm)Add all 4 sides: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 cm
Counting squares to find the perimeterCount the sides of the squares around the edge
Counting a corner square only onceA corner square has 2 sides on the edge
Mixing up area and perimeterArea = squares inside. Perimeter = distance around
Counting every part square as a whole oneCount only squares that are half or more covered
Writing cm for an areaArea is in squares, cm² or m². Perimeter is in cm or m

faq.q: What do Year 4 students learn about perimeter and area in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: They recognise ways of measuring perimeter and area (AC9M4M02): adding the side lengths for perimeter, and counting square units, including half squares, for area. They meet cm² and m² and estimate the area of irregular shapes on a grid.

faq.q: What is the difference between perimeter and area?
faq.a: Perimeter is the distance around the outside of a shape, measured in cm or m. Area is the space inside, measured in square units such as cm² or m².

faq.q: How do you estimate the area of an irregular shape on a grid?
faq.a: Count the whole squares, then count each square that is half or more covered as 1. Leave out the squares that are less than half covered.

faq.q: Do Year 4 students use length × width for area?
faq.a: Not as a formula yet. They count squares, and seeing that 3 rows of 5 squares is 3 × 5 = 15 is a good shortcut that leads to the formula in later years.

sets.title: Area: count squares and half squares

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: There are 15 whole squares and 1 half square. 1 half square is ½ of a square. 15 + ½ = 15½ cm².

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: Count the squares inside: 4 rows of 6 squares. 4 × 6 = 24 cm². (20 is the number of 1-unit sides around the edge: that is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: there are 8, so the area is 8 squares. Count each square once.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: Count the squares inside: 5 rows of 3 squares. 5 × 3 = 15 cm². (16 is the number of 1-unit sides around the edge: that is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: there are 12, so the area is 12 squares. Count each square once.

items.q: What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: Count the squares inside: 3 rows of 2 squares. 3 × 2 = 6 squares. (10 is the number of 1-unit sides around the edge: that is the perimeter.)

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: there are 14, so the area is 14 cm². Count each square once. (24 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of the shaded shape? Two half squares make one whole square.
items.e: There are 19 whole squares and 1 half square. 1 half square is ½ of a square. 19 + ½ = 19½ squares.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: there are 9, so the area is 9 cm². Count each square once. (16 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded trapezium?
items.e: There are 12 whole squares and 3 half squares. 3 halves make 1½ squares. 12 + 1½ = 13½ cm².

items.q: What is the area of the shaded house shape? Two half squares make one whole square.
items.e: There are 14 whole squares and 4 half squares. 4 halves make 2 squares. 14 + 2 = 16 squares.

items.q: Jack makes a rectangle from square cards. It has 5 rows with 7 cards in each row. What is its area in squares?
items.e: Count the squares, or count in rows: 5 rows of 7 is 5 × 7 = 35 squares.

items.q: Ava makes a rectangle from square tiles. It has 4 rows with 6 tiles in each row. What is its area in squares?
items.e: Count the squares, or count in rows: 4 rows of 6 is 4 × 6 = 24 squares.

items.q: What is the area of the shaded diamond shape? Two half squares make one whole square.
items.e: There are 4 whole squares and 8 half squares. 8 halves make 4 squares. 4 + 4 = 8 squares.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: there are 9, so the area is 9 cm². Count each square once. (14 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: William makes a rectangle from square sticky notes. It has 3 rows with 8 notes in each row. What is its area in squares?
items.e: Count the squares, or count in rows: 3 rows of 8 is 3 × 8 = 24 squares.

items.q: What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: there are 10, so the area is 10 squares. Count each square once.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded triangle?
items.e: There are 6 whole squares and 4 half squares. 4 halves make 2 squares. 6 + 2 = 8 cm².

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the shaded squares, row by row: there are 14, so the area is 14 cm². Count each square once. (18 cm is the perimeter.)

items.q: What is the area of the shaded rectangle?
items.e: Count the squares inside: 3 rows of 7 squares. 3 × 7 = 21 squares. (20 is the number of 1-unit sides around the edge: that is the perimeter.)

sets.title: Estimate area and choose the unit

items.q: Harper covers her desk with sticky notes, with no gaps or overlaps. She uses 4 rows of 6 notes. What is the area of her desk in sticky notes?
items.e: 4 rows of 6: 4 × 6 = 24 sticky notes. 20 is the number of notes around the edge (the perimeter idea); 10 is only 4 + 6.
Whole squares: 5. Squares half or more covered: 10. Estimate: 5 + 10 = 15 cm². Squares less than half covered (8) are not counted.

items.q: Leo and Mia both cover the same table with paper squares. Leo needs 12 squares. Mia needs 48 squares. Why?
items.e: It is the same table, so the area is the same. Smaller squares are needed in bigger numbers. That is why we use a standard unit such as cm² or m².
Whole squares: 5. Squares half or more covered: 6. Estimate: 5 + 6 = 11 cm². Squares less than half covered (12) are not counted.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of a classroom floor?
items.e: A floor is big and we cover the space inside it, so use square metres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of a netball court?
items.e: A netball court is big and area is the space inside, so use square metres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the perimeter of the school basketball court?
items.e: Perimeter is a length around the edge. A court is big, so use metres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: About how big is the floor of a classroom?
items.e: A classroom is roughly 8 m by 8 m: 8 rows of 8 one-metre squares is 64, so about 60 m². 6 m² is a small rug, 600 m² is bigger than a netball court.

items.q: You estimate the area of a curved shape on a squared grid. Which squares do you count?
c: Whole and half or more covered
items.e: Count every whole square, and count a square as 1 if half or more of it is covered. Leave out squares that are less than half covered. The bits you count and leave out roughly balance.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of a page in your maths book?
items.e: A page is small and area is the space inside, so use square centimetres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the area of a postage stamp?
items.e: A stamp is small and we cover the space inside it, so use square centimetres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². Which shape has the smallest area?
items.e: Count the squares in each shape: A 11, B 8, C 7, D 10. Shape C has the smallest area (7 cm²).
Whole squares: 10. Squares half or more covered: 9. Estimate: 10 + 9 = 19 m². Squares less than half covered (11) are not counted.

items.q: Each shape has an area of 8 cm². Which shape has the longest perimeter?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides around each shape: A 14 cm, B 18 cm, C 12 cm, D 12 cm. The same area can have different perimeters. Shape B has the longest (18 cm).
Whole squares: 6. Squares half or more covered: 7. Estimate: 6 + 7 = 13 cm². Squares less than half covered (13) are not counted.

items.q: Which unit is best for measuring the perimeter of a photo?
items.e: Perimeter is a length around the edge. A photo is small, so use centimetres. cm and m are for lengths; cm² and m² are for areas.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². Which shape has the largest area?
items.e: Count the squares in each shape: A 7, B 8, C 5, D 9. Shape D has the largest area (9 cm²).
Whole squares: 6. Squares half or more covered: 5. Estimate: 6 + 5 = 11 cm². Squares less than half covered (12) are not counted.

items.q: About how big is the cover of an exercise book?
items.e: An exercise book is about 25 cm by 20 cm: 20 rows of 25 one-centimetre squares is 500 cm². Area needs a square unit, and 50 m² would be a whole room.
Whole squares: 8. Squares half or more covered: 7. Estimate: 8 + 7 = 15 cm². Squares less than half covered (12) are not counted.

sets.title: Word problems: fences, gardens and carpet

items.q: A classroom floor plan is drawn on a grid. Each square is 1 m². The floor covers 30 whole squares and 4 half squares. What is the area of the floor?
items.e: Two half squares make one whole square, so 4 half squares make 2. Area: 30 + 2 = 32 m².

items.q: Liam’s family builds a square chook pen with sides of 6 m. Each fence panel is 2 m long. How many panels go all the way around?
items.e: Perimeter: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 m. Each panel is 2 m: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 panels.

items.q: At the athletics carnival warm-up, Kai jogs 2 times around a rectangular field. The field is 60 m long and 40 m wide. How far does he jog?
items.e: Once around: 60 + 40 + 60 + 40 = 200 m. Two times around: 2 × 200 = 400 m.

items.q: Mia glues ribbon around the edge of a photo frame. The frame is 20 cm long and 15 cm wide. How much ribbon does she need?
items.e: Ribbon goes around the edge, so find the perimeter: 20 + 15 + 20 + 15 = 70 cm.

items.q: The school basketball court is 28 m long and 15 m wide. The class jogs once around the edge. How far is that?
items.e: Once around is the perimeter: 28 + 15 + 28 + 15 = 86 m.

items.q: A pinboard in the classroom is 120 cm long and 90 cm wide. The teacher staples a paper border around the edge. How long is the border?
items.e: Border around the edge = perimeter: 120 + 90 + 120 + 90 = 420 cm.

items.q: Isla’s family is building a garden bed 4 m long and 2 m wide. How much timber edging goes all the way around it?
items.e: The edging goes along all 4 sides: 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 12 m.

items.q: A square sandpit has a perimeter of 20 m. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m. Check: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 m.

items.q: A school vegetable patch is marked into 1 m squares: 6 rows of 4 squares. Tomatoes grow in 5 squares and lettuce in the rest. What area is lettuce?
items.e: Whole patch: 6 × 4 = 24 m². Take away the tomatoes: 24 − 5 = 19 m².

items.q: A rectangular vegetable garden is 12 m long and 8 m wide. A fence goes all the way around, except for a gate that is 2 m wide. How much fence is needed?
items.e: Perimeter: 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 m. There is no fence across the gate: 40 − 2 = 38 m.

items.q: This is the plan of an L-shaped garden bed. How much edging goes all the way around it?
items.e: Missing side: 13 − 6 = 7 m. Add all 6 sides: 7 + 4 + 6 + 3 + 13 + 7 = 40 m.

items.q: The teacher has 20 carpet squares. Each is 1 m². The reading corner needs 4 rows of 4 squares. How many carpet squares are left over?
items.e: Reading corner: 4 rows of 4 = 16 squares. Left over: 20 − 16 = 4 squares.

items.q: A cricket pitch is about 20 m long and 3 m wide. The groundskeeper walks once around its edge. About how far is that?
items.e: Perimeter: 20 + 3 + 20 + 3 = 46 m. 60 is 20 × 3, which is the area in m².

items.q: A rectangular flower bed has a perimeter of 30 m. One side is 9 m long. How long is the side next to it?
items.e: The two 9 m sides make 18 m. 30 − 18 = 12 m for the other two sides, so each is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m. Check: 9 + 6 + 9 + 6 = 30 m.

items.q: Ruby has 16 m of fence to make a rectangular pen for her guinea pigs. Which pen gives them the most space?
items.e: All four pens use 16 m of fence. Count the 1 m squares inside: 7 × 1 = 7, 6 × 2 = 12, 5 × 3 = 15, 4 × 4 = 16 m². The square has the most space.

items.q: Oliver wants to put coloured tape around the edge of a poster. What should he work out?
items.e: Tape goes around the edge, so find the perimeter. Perimeter is a length, so it is in cm.

items.q: Zara’s bedroom floor is 4 m by 3 m. Carpet squares are 1 m by 1 m. How many carpet squares cover the floor?
items.e: 3 rows of 4 squares: 3 × 4 = 12 carpet squares, so the area is 12 m². 14 is the perimeter in metres (4 + 3 + 4 + 3).

items.q: Harper wants to cover the front of a book with contact paper. What should she work out?
items.e: Covering the space inside a shape is area. Area is counted in squares, so it is in cm².

items.q: A classroom floor is covered with square carpet tiles. Each tile is 1 m long and 1 m wide. There are 7 rows of 9 tiles. What is the area of the floor?
items.e: Each tile is 1 m², so count the tiles: 7 rows of 9 is 7 × 9 = 63 m².

items.q: Amelia has 1 m of ribbon. She puts ribbon around the edge of a card that is 20 cm by 12 cm. How much ribbon is left?
items.e: 1 m = 100 cm. Perimeter of the card: 20 + 12 + 20 + 12 = 64 cm. Left: 100 − 64 = 36 cm.
